# `unittest` and test discipline

A test that never runs proves nothing. Nim ships `unittest` in the standard library, so there is no
package to install. This chapter writes tests that actually run, then reads their output. What you
take away is not the framework but the habit of running it every time the code changes.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can write `suite` and `test` blocks, use `check`, `require`, and `expect`,
read passing and failing output, and recognize `undeclared identifier` when `std/unittest` is not
imported.
:::

## Suites and tests

Save the following as `tests.nim`, then run `nim c -r tests.nim`.

```{.nim}
import std/unittest

proc add(a, b: int): int =
  a + b

suite "add":
  test "adds two positive numbers":
    check add(2, 3) == 5

  test "adds a negative number":
    check add(-1, 4) == 3
```

```{.txt}

[Suite] add
  [OK] adds two positive numbers
  [OK] adds a negative number
```

Three things are worth noticing.

- `suite` groups tests. Its name appears in the output behind `[Suite]`.
- `test` is one case. Every passing case prints `[OK]`, indented two spaces.
- The first line of the output really is empty. That is `unittest`'s default, not a typo in this
  book.

`check` takes a `bool` expression; if it is `false`, the test is marked failed. That is why the
comparison goes in as-is, not as a string or some other value.

Name a test after behavior, not after a procedure. `"adds two positive numbers"` is more useful than
`"test add"`, because when a test fails, that name is what shows up in the output and points to the
promise that broke. A good name makes a failure readable without opening the code.

## `check`, `require`, and `expect`

`check` is the main tool. It may appear several times in one `test`, and all of them must pass for
the test to print `[OK]`.

```{.nim}
import std/unittest

proc isEven(n: int): bool =
  n mod 2 == 0

suite "isEven":
  test "catches even numbers":
    check isEven(0)
    check isEven(2)
    check isEven(42)

  test "rejects odd numbers":
    check not isEven(1)
    check not isEven(7)
```

```{.txt}

[Suite] isEven
  [OK] catches even numbers
  [OK] rejects odd numbers
```

To stop in the middle of a test, use `require`. The difference from `check`: `check` records the
failure but keeps going through the rest of the test. `require` stops the whole run right there, so
`teardown` does not get to run either. Use `require` when the next step makes no sense without the
previous one, for example dividing by a value you just proved is not zero.

`expect` checks that a block raises an exception of a given type. The block must not pass silently;
if it does, the test fails. This is how you test the error path, not only the happy path.

```{.nim}
import std/unittest

proc divide(a, b: int): int =
  if b == 0:
    raise newException(ValueError, "division by zero")
  a div b

suite "divide":
  test "returns the quotient":
    check divide(10, 2) == 5

  test "rejects a zero divisor":
    expect ValueError:
      discard divide(1, 0)

  test "keeps running after a passing require":
    require divide(9, 3) == 3
    check true
```

```{.txt}

[Suite] divide
  [OK] returns the quotient
  [OK] rejects a zero divisor
  [OK] keeps running after a passing require
```

Those three tools cover most tests. Their output is the same: `[OK]` for a passing test.

When every case needs the same starting state, `unittest` provides `setup` and `teardown`. The
`setup` block runs before each `test`, and `teardown` after it. Both are written inside the `suite`
block; at the top level the names are not recognized. Use them when each test needs fresh data, such as a temporary file that must be
created and removed again.

## Deliberate error: forgetting to import `std/unittest`

`suite`, `test`, and `check` are not part of the language. They all come from `std/unittest`.

```{.nim}
suite "add":
  test "adds two numbers":
    check 1 + 1 == 2
```

```{.txt}
tests.nim(1, 1) Error: undeclared identifier: 'suite'
```

The message points at line 1, column 1: the first letter of `suite`. `undeclared identifier` means
the name is unknown in every scope. The fix is to add `import std/unittest` on the first line.

This is the same pattern as any other module. Standard-library names never arrive on their own; they
must be imported first. A time-saving habit is to write the `import` lines at the top before writing
the tests. In a nimble project, test files live in the `tests/` folder, and `nimble test` runs them
all. The contents stay the same: `unittest`, and a non-zero exit code when something fails.

## When a test fails

A failing test prints a `[FAILED]` line, and above it a `Check failed:` line carrying the file,
line, column, and the values compared. The process also exits with a non-zero code.

That exit code is what matters for automation. CI does not read the text; it only checks whether the
process succeeded. As long as one test fails, the whole process counts as failed, and the merge is
held. That is what turns a test suite into a gate rather than a report.

## Exercises

1. Write a `suite` for a procedure that computes factorials, with three cases: zero, one, and five.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   import std/unittest

   suite "strings":
     test "length":
       check "nim".len == 3
     test "first char":
       check "nim"[0] == 'n'
   ```
3. The code below fails to compile. Fix it and explain the message:
   ```{.nim}
   import std/unittest

   suite "math":
     test "one":
       check 1 + 1
   ```
4. Run a `test` that uses `expect` for an exception that is never raised. Explain why the test fails.

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

## Summary

- `unittest` is in the standard library; no package to install.
- `suite` groups, `test` marks one case, and `check` compares a `bool` expression.
- `require` stops the whole run early; `expect` makes sure an exception is raised.
- A passing test prints `[OK]`, a failing one `[FAILED]`, and a failing run exits non-zero.
- A missing `import std/unittest` gives an `undeclared identifier` at compile time.
